traps.excerpt: Interview P06 was entirely excluded due to severe research-method flaws
While the phrasing in P02:t8 was templated across several transcripts
Solo Student Households (out-of-target contrast; sample size: 1 interview: P07)
Retired Couples with Fixed Routines (in-target demographic, but no problem fit; sample size: 1 interview: P09)
A single stated claim of 30 euros per month from adjacent participant P08 was anchored to an isolated holiday spoilage incident and is excluded as an extreme outlier
A1 (Usability risk, Riskiest assumption): Households will reliably input and maintain an up-to-date fridge and pantry inventory
While weekly shoppers follow plans, households with irregular schedules abandon weekly planning apps and feel guilt when plans fall apart
The idea brief claim that dinner planning causes couples to argue is weakly supported
Competitor benchmarking shows that the idea brief's claim that existing recipe apps do not know what you already own is contradicted by direct market evidence
The claim that meal-planning software is growing at 25% annually is unsupported
What is the objectively measured food waste and grocery spend over time, rather than self-reported estimates

criteria.justification: The brief answers all six required questions in complete, substantial detail, ensuring nothing is left out.
Claims are heavily cited and grounded, explicitly detailing raw counts, weighted support, and distinguishing observed behavior from stated preferences.
The brief is perfectly calibrated, cautiously evaluating unvalidated metrics (like willingness to pay) and immediately rejecting unreliable assumptions and overclaims.
The next steps are exceptionally clear and actionable, detailing participant recruitment, success metrics, test methods, and explicit thresholds for go/no-go pivot decisions.
The text is tight, concise, and structured logically with clear headings and bullet points, making it highly readable and actionable for product teams.
